name: Esther Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner in an underground potash mine. Potash is a salt they turn into fertiliser, and the continuous miner is a big machine with spinning drums covered in teeth that chews straight into the ore, no blasting, and loads it onto a conveyor behind. We go down in the cage at seven, about a kilometre deep, and I cut rooms for about nine hours, following the laser lines and checking the cutting profile on a little screen in the cab. I like that it's very precise, you're shaping a tunnel almost like a sculptor, and what wears me out is the heat down there and the long walk to the lunch room.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Joel, he does software testing for a logistics company in town. We've got a bit over a year of expenses saved and some shares. I fly drones on weekends, I got my commercial drone licence last year, and I do survey flights for a couple of farms, mapping fields so they know where to put fertiliser. I use AI every day, for work notes, for planning drone flights, for meal plans, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief for some people and a bit boring for others. At work I'd probably say I'm still using it every day for small stuff, which is true. Online I'd post something about how the tools are still useful even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much. The mine's been moving towards remote-controlled continuous miners for years, AI or not, so that keeps happening slowly. I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep growing the drone stuff on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for planning and notes, and I'd put more time into the drone business, maybe pick up two or three more farm clients this year. I'd sign up for the remote-control trial the mine keeps talking about. Keep saving, keep the shares as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, honestly, I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the drone work. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle has a farm about an hour out, and he was complaining that he didn't know which bits of his fields needed fertiliser. I found a drone course, used AI to help me study for the licence, and mapped his whole farm on a Sunday. It's funny, I dig the fertiliser out of the ground on weekdays and tell farmers where to put it on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at the mine know about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few people. My shift boss thinks it's cool and asked if I could fly the surface stockpiles one day. The older guys think I'm mad for working weekends when the mine pays this well.

S0.say: She'd call it a relief for some and a bit boring for others, tell the crew she still uses AI daily for small things, and post that the tools are useful even if not magic.
S0.think: She thinks it wouldn't change much, since the mine is moving to remote-controlled continuous miners slowly anyway. She'd keep doing her job and growing the drone work on the side.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for planning and notes and aims to add two or three more farm clients to her drone business this year. Signs up for the mine's remote-control trial and keeps saving.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly disappointed, because she enjoys new tools.
S0.quote: It's funny, I dig the fertiliser out of the ground on weekdays and tell farmers where to put it on weekends.
S0.fieldNote: Esther already has a working side business, drone mapping for farms, built partly by studying with AI. She enjoys the irony of mining fertiliser and then guiding where it goes. She's comfortable with automation and slightly bored by a world where nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but people can handle it if they're given time and training. At work I'd be helping the others set up the new tools. Online I'd post practical stuff, like here's a course that's actually worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think this is good for me. I'm the one who likes the screens, so I'm likely to end up in the remote room or on the data side. The drone work could grow too, if farms are getting more high-tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd do every course the mine offered on remote operation and data. I'd look at whether the mine needs someone to fly the underground drones they use for inspecting old rooms, which is a real job at some mines. I'd also put some savings into a few companies that make mining automation gear, because if it's happening anyway, I want a slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lunch buddy Gary. He's fifty-one, and he's a brilliant operator, but he flips his phone face down whenever I show him something new. I'd try to drag Gary along with me, but you can't make someone learn if they've decided they're too old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in automation companies. Doesn't that feel strange, betting on the thing replacing your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But the machines are coming whether I buy the shares or not. I'd rather own a little piece of it than just watch it happen.

S1.say: She'd say people can handle a big change with time and training, help colleagues set up new tools and post practical tips like which courses are worth doing.
S1.think: She thinks this is good for her, as someone who likes screens and is likely to move to the remote room or the data side. She expects her drone work could grow as farms go high-tech.
S1.do: Takes every remote operation and data course the mine offers in the first six months and looks into flying underground inspection drones. Puts some savings into companies that make mining automation equipment.
S1.quote: I'd try to drag Gary along with me, but you can't make someone learn if they've decided they're too old.
S1.fieldNote: She's openly pragmatic about investing in the automation replacing her crew: the machines come either way, so she'd rather own a slice. Her concern is Gary, who has decided he's too old to learn. She already sees specific new roles, like underground inspection drones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and it's too fast, and the government needs to put a safety net in place right now. At work I'd be telling people to save every cent they can. Online I'd post a lot of practical advice, but I'd also be honest that nobody really knows what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. My whole edge is that I'm good with tech, but if AI can do anything, my edge doesn't matter much. I'd have savings and shares, and I think the shares in AI and robot companies would probably go up, so financially I'd be okay for a while, but I'd have no idea what job I'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move more savings into shares in the companies building the robots, carefully, maybe another fifteen percent. I'd keep the drone business going as long as farms paid for it, but I'd expect drones to fly themselves soon. Joel and I would talk about moving to a bigger city where there might be more new kinds of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. More like my brain is running at full speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze every bit of money out of the mine and the drones, and get into any job that's about checking or signing off on what the robots do. Two years is about how long it took me to build the drone thing. I'd have to watch it get built and taken away in the same stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving to a city. What makes you think there'd be more there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, honestly. It's a guess. More people means more weird new jobs, I think, and Joel's work is there anyway. But I'm not sure it'd be better, I'd just be trying something rather than waiting.

S2.say: She'd say it's huge and too fast and the government needs a safety net now. She'd tell coworkers to save and post practical advice online while admitting nobody knows what's coming.
S2.think: It worries her because her edge with technology stops mattering if AI can do anything. Financially she expects to be okay for a while, partly because AI and robot company shares might rise, but she'd have no idea what job she'd have.
S2.do: Moves about fifteen percent more of her savings into shares in companies building robots and keeps the drone business while farms still pay. Talks with Joel about moving to a bigger city and seeks roles checking or signing off on robots' work.
S2.feel: Anxious but not frozen, with her mind racing.
S2.quote: Two years is about how long it took me to build the drone thing. I'd have to watch it get built and taken away in the same stretch.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens the thing she's built her confidence on, her comfort with tech. She responds by acting rather than waiting, including a possible city move she admits is a guess. Her investment logic becomes a kind of hedge against her own job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, and people should start now. At work I'd be running little sessions showing people how to use the tools. Online, the same as before, practical stuff, less panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to reposition. I'd be thirty-two, with experience in remote ops and drones, and maybe a business that's about using AI rather than competing with it. It's still scary that it can do anything, but I'd have time to find a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short course in data analysis, the kind where you work out what the numbers from machines actually mean. I'd grow the drone business into a farm data service, so it's less about flying and more about advice. I'd keep investing a bit in automation companies and keep a year of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to change what I sell. With two years I'm selling drone flights that a drone will soon do itself. With five, I'm selling the farmer someone to trust, and that's harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think farmers would still want a person, if AI can do the advice too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. My uncle wouldn't take advice from a screen if it was free. But his son would. So maybe I'd have ten years of customers like my uncle, and then that's it, I don't know.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to make a plan and people should start now. She'd run sessions at work showing people the tools and keep posting practical, calmer advice online.
S3.think: She thinks five years gives her time to reposition, landing at thirty-two with remote ops and drone experience and maybe a business that uses AI rather than competing with it. It's still scary, but she'd have time to find a gap.
S3.do: Takes a short data analysis course in the first year and turns the drone business into a farm data and advice service. Keeps investing a little in automation companies and keeps a year of cash.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: With two years I'm selling drone flights that a drone will soon do itself. With five, I'm selling the farmer someone to trust, and that's harder to replace.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she plans to shift from selling a task to selling trust, a smart move she then questions herself. Her uncle versus his son captures her uncertainty about how long human advice lasts. She keeps a year of cash even while investing, which suits her centre, practical outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it is wasting it. At work I'd be fairly upbeat, and I'd be pushing for the mine to start training people early. Online I'd be the one posting long threads about what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels good for someone my age. I'd be thirty-seven, with a decade of building things up. I'd worry for people who can't or won't change, but I wouldn't be worried about myself much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the continuous miner for a few years and move into the remote room when it opens. I'd grow the farm data business slowly, maybe go part-time at the mine by year four or five. I'd keep investing and make sure that by the end, I've got enough in shares that the money works even when I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and kind of excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by the end you'd want money working without you. Is that the real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of. If AI can do everything, the people who own a piece of it are fine and the people who don't are in trouble. Ten years is long enough for an ordinary miner like me to own a small slice, if I start this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shares went bad, or if the government did something like tax them really heavily. I'd be fine with a fair tax, honestly, as long as there's something left for the people who saved.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift that shouldn't be wasted, stay upbeat at work and push the mine to train people early. Online she'd post long threads about what to learn.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is good for someone her age, giving her a decade to build things before thirty-seven. She'd worry about people who can't or won't change, but not much about herself.
S4.do: Keeps running the continuous miner for a few years, moves to the remote room when it opens and grows the farm data business, possibly going part-time by year four or five. Keeps investing so that her shares can support her by the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for an ordinary miner like me to own a small slice, if I start this month.
S4.fieldNote: Her deepest plan is ownership: she believes those who hold a piece of AI will be fine. She'd accept a fair tax on it, which fits her centre outlook. Time turns her from defensive to energised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan is built on being early and flexible, and with two years everyone's caught at once. What would help is a clear government plan for income support and easy access to training, and honestly, just someone telling us the truth about what's coming. I can handle bad news. What I can't handle is finding out from a robot that's already parked in my spot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me can do for others. I'd be happy to teach the older guys stuff. Nobody's asked me to.

headlineQuote: I can handle bad news. What I can't handle is finding out from a robot that's already parked in my spot.
portrait: Esther is a 27-year-old continuous miner operator at an underground potash mine who lives with her partner Joel and has over a year's savings and some shares. She uses AI every day and runs a weekend drone mapping business for farms, which she built partly by studying with AI. She sees most change as an opening and plans to move into remote operations, grow the drone work into farm advice, and invest in automation companies. Only AGI in two years makes her anxious, because it catches everyone at once and wipes out her edge with technology; with ten years she's excited.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her plan depends on being early and flexible and everyone would be caught at once.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government plan for income support, easy access to training, and honest information about what's coming.
